item.title: Champi now a Cat 4 typhoon, expected to have winds of 150 mph when it passes near southern Guam
item.description: Typhoon Champi has rapidly intensified and is now a Category 4 typhoon, expected to pass just south of Guam between 4 and 5 a.m. Sunday with 150 mph winds. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center said Champi currently has winds of 130 miles and gusts to 161 mph. It is continuing in a period of rapid intensification.
item.content:encoded:
Typhoon Champi has rapidly intensified and is now a Category 4 typhoon, expected to pass just south of Guam between 4 and 5 a.m. Sunday with 150 mph winds.

The Joint Typhoon Warning Center said Champi currently has winds of 130 miles and gusts to 161 mph. It is continuing in a period of rapid intensification.

As of 4 p.m., Champi was located near 12.5 degrees north latitude and 147.3 degrees east longitude. It was heading to the west-northwest at 15 mph.

Guam has been in Condition of Readiness 1 since 1 p.m. Emergency officials urged residents to stay inside a sturdy, concrete-reinforced structure until COR 4 is announced.

Do not go outside during the storm, even if conditions temporarily appear calm.

Residents in coastal and flood-prone areas should evacuate to safe shelter. Life-threatening coastal flooding is expected.

Rain and winds will deteriorate significantly overnight Saturday. Dangerous, potentially life-threatening conditions may develop rapidly once winds arrive.

item.title: GPA will not turn off power, but customers should expect outages as storm hits Guam
item.description: Guam Power Authority says it will not shut down the islandwide power system as Typhoon Champi bears down on the island. GPA’s goal is to keep part of the system running throughout the typhoon because it will allow for faster post-typhoon recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Guam Power Authority says it will not shut down the islandwide power system as Typhoon Champi bears down on the island.

GPA’s goal is to keep part of the system running throughout the typhoon because it will allow for faster post-typhoon recovery.

Power outages and fluctuations are expected during damaging wind conditions. The system runs automatically and only shuts down power service to residents and businesses when damage has occurred to any of the power circuits/feeders.

Any necessary repairs to the system will resume once high winds subside to a safe level.

If power circuits/feeders go offline, GPA will work on energizing them immediately. If power doesn’t return in a few minutes, it is most likely that the circuit/feeder is damaged and GPA will have to wait until the typhoon passes before it can make repairs.

During extreme weather conditions, dispatchers will receive calls for emergency power situations such as down energized (sparking) lines, damaged poles or blown transformers.

Please stay away from all downed lines and equipment as they may still be energized and can cause harm if you come in contact with them. Consider such situations as dangerous and life-threatening.

If such conditions are present, you can report this situation to GPA's 24-Hour Trouble Dispatch at 671-475-1472/3/4 or via direct message on GPA’s Facebook page. Please provide the exact location or address, contact information and location.

item.title: 'A significant hit for us': Guam residents advised to seek safe shelter, stay away from water
item.description: Announcements were made for residents in southern coastal areas to evacuate, with an emergency shelter opening at Inalahan Middle School at 2 p.m. as Typhoon Champi rapidly intensified Saturday. In a briefing late Saturday morning, Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said the storm, which was forecast to pass over or near the southern part of the island Sunday morning, would be stronger
item.content:encoded:
Announcements were made for residents in southern coastal areas to evacuate, with an emergency shelter opening at Inalahan Middle School at 2 p.m. as Typhoon Champi rapidly intensified Saturday.

In a briefing late Saturday morning, Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said the storm, which was forecast to pass over or near the southern part of the island Sunday morning, would be stronger than Typhoon Mawar was for residents of the south.

“This is going to be a significant hit for us,” he said. “We're going to have a rough day tomorrow.”

He said severe tropical storm-force winds would be felt throughout the island, and they will exceed what Guam experienced during Typhoon Sinlaku in April or Bavi in July.

“Even if this passes over the southern coastal waters, that northern eyewall will pass over the southern villages of Guam, bringing those most intense wind conditions,” he said.

He advised residents to be in safe shelters by sundown.

"Make sure when the sun sets tonight that you are in a hardened shelter," he said. "Reinforced concrete walls. Reinforced concrete roof. If you're not in that, you need to be in a safe shelter, not a tent, canopy tarp, wood-and-tin shelters. These are not going to provide protection by any means with Typhoon Champi."

Emergency managers emphasized that ocean waters would be deadly.

Conditions were deteriorating along coastal waters by late morning.

“If you're along the windward coastal areas of southern eastern Guam, you need to make sure you're away from the coastal areas, away from the water, because we're going to see some surge - upwards of 5 to 7 feet of surge,” Aydlett said. “That's water above normal water levels, but those wind swells, those waves will keep pushing the water higher up onto normally dry ground. So we're going to see a lot of coastal impacts along the windward coasts.”

He said sea and surf conditions would begin to improve on Sunday night and into Monday.

“But again, stay out of the water, stay away from the coast, the surf, the reefs,” he said. “That's going to be dangerous and deadly out there through the day on Sunday.”

item.title: Trump promised a swing district blitz. He's going to a lot of very red states
item.description: 📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.
item.content:encoded:
📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Early in September, President Trump gathered Republicans running in competitive races for a dinner in the White House Rose Garden. Prime aged beef burgers were on the menu as the president made a pledge to spend the final month before the midterms campaigning for the approximately 30 Republican candidates in attendance.

" I'm going to go to every one of those 35 places and we're going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump said confidently.

The White House hasn't clarified which 35 places the president was talking about that night. Since then, Trump has campaigned with fewer than a third of those candidates. Rather than focus on swing states and swing districts as the president said he would, his travel schedule has taken him to a lot of Republican territory.

Trump's itinerary is both a reflection of where he can help (and where he can't) but also of a shifting landscape where even red state Republicans need a boost.

On the tarmac between rally stops in Arizona and Montana this week, Trump attempted to spin his visits to states he won decisively just two years ago as a matter of gratitude.

"So, I do it to thank them," Trump said. "I also do it because we have some great people there that are running and I want to make sure they win."

He went on to bemoan the drop in Republican turnout in years when he isn't on the ballot, something Trump and his team are trying to counteract with an October campaign rally blitz that has taken him to Ohio (twice), Texas (twice), Oklahoma and even Tennessee.

"What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?" Trump mused from stage to wild cheers.

Earlier this week, the president took an eight hour flight to Alaska to campaign for Republicans, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich, both of whom face races that are too close for comfort in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

"This is worth the 8 hours in a plane," Trump said to an adoring crowd. "And don't forget I've got 8 hours going back. Give me credit for that."

In fact, he made two more stops on the way back and spent the night at the Trump hotel in Las Vegas.

The Republican National Committee has announced he'll be campaigning in Kansas Monday, which has a toss-up U.S. Senate race, something few would have anticipated even a month ago.

Republicans are on defense in a lot of states where they've traditionally won without much trouble. Trump's team is picking locations where he can activate the Republican base in places where he's done well in the past.

"Just a lot of excitement, a lot of momentum building up on the ground here," said RNC Chairman Joe Gruters in a call with NPR from a Trump rally in Arizona. "It's turnout, turnout, turnout. How do you get the base to show up? You put the president on the ballot. You put him out there."

Trump frequently implores his supporters to vote as if he were on the ballot. It's a novel political strategy that runs counter to the norm for unpopular presidents whose parties face significant midterm headwinds. Trump claims the polls are wrong about his underwater approval rating.

As for Trump's message, it doesn't change much from stop to stop. There are the greatest hits: his past election wins, his One Big Beautiful Bill, and a walk down memory lane from right before he launched the war with Iran when gas prices were cheaper. He teases a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the House and the Senate, an idea he first rolled out at the unconventional Republican midterm convention, but has faced resistance from elected Republicans. On most stops he talks about a specific project or deal he has planned for the state.

On Tuesday, Trump is set to campaign in Greenville, North Carolina. Republican campaign committees have already started canceling ad reservations meant to help Trump's handpicked Republican Senate candidate there, Michael Whatley. It's a sign they see that race as moving out of reach.

There's also a congressional district in Eastern North Carolina that was redrawn to favor Republicans as part of Trump's mid-decade redistricting push. It shouldn't be competitive, but it's now rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.

"I think it's going to backfire on them this year in every way shape and form," said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. "He's trying to drum up any amount of support that he can at the last minute. But I don't think that North Carolinians are going to fall for it again."

item.title: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know

item.content:encoded:
No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.

On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections , and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.

The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations , including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.

No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.

"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."

There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.

The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls , and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.

Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour .

All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.

Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.

"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."

Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.

Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.

At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians , a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.

"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

item.content:encoded:
DELHI, India — At 2 a.m. on the sidewalk outside one of Delhi's best-known public hospitals, Shabana Kumar gently wakes her husband. They sleep in shifts of about an hour at a time because their 6-year-old son is a patient in the oncology ward, being treated for leukemia, a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. They are afraid that if they are both asleep, an urgent call could come about their son's condition and they might miss it.

The Kumar family lives more than 600 miles from Delhi in the state of Bihar. Arun, 32, works as a farmer. Shabana, 30, is a homemaker caring for their only son.

They made the trip to Delhi because they could not afford the cost of their child's cancer treatment in Bihar. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, or AIIMS, subsidizes expenses for families in need.

But for many families, there is one challenge they must bear on their own — finding a place to live in Delhi during the days, weeks, even months of treatment. Like the Kumars, families who can't afford to rent lodging often set up a temporary dwelling on the sidewalk.

On a night in August, dozens of families were sleeping on blankets or sheets spread directly on the sidewalk. Some tie mosquito nets to railings to protect themselves and their kids. They keep their bags and other belongings beside them as they sleep.

During the day, families move between the sidewalk and the hospital for appointments, tests, medicines and consultations. They carry their most important belongings with them while leaving less valuable items at their sleeping spot. One family member often stays behind to keep an eye on their things.

Like the family from Bihar, people who've accompanied a patient may sleep outside while the patient is housed in the hospital. In other cases, the person receiving care is seen during the day but does not have a bed, so they sleep on the sidewalk as well.

At night, the sidewalk dwellers return to the pavement, where a small ecosystem has grown around the families. Women cook rice over makeshift brick stoves. Volunteers distribute food. Nearby shops sell medicines and other necessities. Nearby tea stalls not only serve beverages but let families charge their phones.

Once strangers, they exchange information about doctors, tests and where to find a free meal or, when none is available, an affordable one they can pay for.

Vishnu Singh, 38, runs a tea stall outside AIIMS.

"I see poor people sleeping here every day, so many that I cannot even count them," he said.

At AIIMS and Safdarjung Hospital, which is associated with Vardhman Mahavir Medical College, we interviewed families who had traveled from across India, often hundreds of miles from home, to seek medical care. The two hospitals stand opposite each other, treating patients with illnesses ranging from cancer and heart conditions to intestinal disorders and other serious ailments.

Some families had been there for a week, others for a month or longer. For many, returning home between hospital visits was impractical, so patients and the relatives accompanying them stayed in Delhi for the duration of their care.

The families we spoke with described their experiences spending days or weeks in Delhi while navigating appointments, tests, consultations and treatment.

It is a startling contrast — a hospital that provides critical care, that, according to its annual report, gives subsidies to thousands of poor families for treatment — and that is ringed by folks who traveled great distances to find care for a loved one and who cannot afford a place to stay.

NPR reached out to the hospital by email to ask about the issue of accommodations and the community of sidewalk dwellers. The hospital did not respond.

AIIMS' website notes that its Medical Social Service Unit provides financial assistance for medical treatment and travel costs for some patients coming from outside Delhi. It also states that the unit helps arrange accommodation for out-of-town patients and their family members and caregivers at dharamshalas , traditional charitable lodging facilities affiliated with AIIMS, or other low-cost accommodation.

The website does not say whether AIIMS pays for those accommodations or provides financial assistance specifically for the lodging costs. Shalini Yadav is one of the patients who sleeps on the sidewalk with her parents.

Yadav is a second-year college student from Piprat village in Tikamgarh district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India. She had been preparing for the state civil service examination. Her plan was to become a government officer.

Now she is spending her days reading Gunahon Ka Devta (The God of Sins) , a famous 1949 Hindi tragic romance novel written by Dharamvir Bharati , on the pavement outside AIIMS, waiting to find out when her treatment will begin and when she can go home.

Yadav says she has been dealing with an intestinal illness for five or six years and has already undergone two operations. Her family had sought treatment elsewhere before relatives and neighbors advised them to travel to Delhi in search of better treatment at AIIMS — a trip of roughly 370 miles. "We thought AIIMS was the best hospital in India," she said. The cost of staying in Delhi was also a burden: Her family could not afford a room and had already spent thousands of rupees on travel and other expenses.

When we interviewed her on Aug. 3, she had been there for about three weeks with her parents, Surendra Singh Yadav, 47, a farmer, and Kalpana Yadav, 45.

"We thought the facilities would be good, the doctors would be good, and everything would happen quickly. We never imagined that we would have to sleep on the road," she said.

For her, the pavement is not just uncomfortable, it is also frightening. During the day, she says, she can manage. At night, she worries about the people around her.

"There are all kinds of people here," she says. "Some are good, but some drink or use drugs. There is shouting and fighting. As a girl, I feel very uncomfortable here at night."

But the family has little choice. They cannot afford a room in Delhi, she says. "We have decided that we have to sleep on the road because there is no other option."

During the day, Yadav goes into the hospital for appointments, tests and checkups, then returns to the pavement while waiting for the next step in her treatment. Everything is on hold — her college education, her hopes of qualifying for a government job, her father's farming work.

"It feels like we are being forced to live like this," she says.

Lakhi Bai, 62, from Ramnagar in Maihar district, Madhya Pradesh, in central India, about 500 miles away, came to Delhi seeking treatment for diabetes and a condition that she says causes numbness and a loss of sensation in parts of her body.

She says she could sometimes sustain an injury without feeling pain. When we met her, she had been sleeping outside Safdarjung Hospital for about 20 days. During that time, she says, she had been going to different doctors and departments for consultations and tests but had not yet received a treatment plan.

item.title: Weddings are expensive. How about a grocery store cake?
item.description: Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000. Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.
item.content:encoded:
Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000.

Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.

"We love Costco, first of all," said Anna Holleran, who got married in California's Bay Area this year — and, yes, picked up her wedding cake from the grocery wholesaler.

"Their cakes are so good," she said. "How can you go wrong?"

Weddings are one of the most expensive days in many people's lives, costing on average about $36,000 , according to the wedding-planning website Zola. The Bank of America Institute reports wedding spending among its customers was up 8.5% in May from a year earlier.

Some of that is by choice, with couples deciding to splurge on the venue or chasing the latest TikTok reception trend. But there are less controllable economic factors too, from inflation driving up the price of suits and catering to tariffs bumping up the cost of imported flowers and bridal gowns .

And according to Emily Forrest, head of communications at Zola, one place where couples are willing to trim costs is the cake. About a third of couples surveyed by Zola said they'd consider spending less on cake and dessert.

"When it comes to a wedding, every couple always has to sit down and say, 'Where are we going to save, and where are we going to splurge?'" said Forrest. "And cakes just don't seem to rise to the splurge occasion for a lot of couples."

What couples aren't willing to do is ditch the cake tradition entirely.

"You can't skip the cake!" said Lily Alana Stewart, who got married last year in central Alabama. "Everybody looks forward to a cake at a wedding."

To save money, she ordered her cake from Publix, a grocery chain in the South.

Stewart used baby's breath for decorating the venue, and Publix incorporated that into the cake design. Her co-workers who attended were surprised to learn where the cake came from. "They said, 'Wait, wait, wait. Your wedding cake was from Publix ?'" Stewart said. "And they were still mind blown."

While the average wedding cake costs about $5.50 a slice, according to Zola, a slice of Publix cake is about $1.50 cheaper, while still pulling off that classic three-tiered, white-frosted wedding cake look. The chain also offers couples a tasting flight, so they can sample four flavors — including red velvet and carrot — before they order.

The wedding cake business has grown at Publix. The stores around Birmingham, Ala., sell about 50% more than they did before 2020, according to Jeff Brancato, a Publix retail improvement specialist. A chocolate cake with fondant that can serve 94 people costs $388, according to the price guide for the Birmingham area.

"There is definitely big savings when it comes to it," Brancato said.

Still, you do get what you pay for in a grocery store cake, including fewer options than what a specialty baker might offer — like more flavors or more customized decorations. While Publix touts its wedding cake business , Costco doesn't even list its half sheet as a wedding cake. It works out to about 70 cents per slice. (Costco did not return NPR's request for an interview.)

Holleran's priority was saving money where she could. Her wedding was near her home in California wine country — a region that's a destination spot for other couples and where venues are expensive.

Holleran said the culinary details of her cake weren't what mattered. "The real point is that you're sharing a dessert for the first time with somebody that you love," she said. "It's kind of symbolic of all the sweet moments that you're supposed to share in a marriage."
